name: component_ablation
notes: research_question: Which components are actually load-bearing? A systematic single-component ablation study over the five core modules (memory, self-model, workspace, metacognition, attention) on the QA calibration task, measuring each module's marginal contribution and verifying graceful degradation.

hypothesis: Ablating any single one of the five components (memory, self_model, workspace, metacognition, attention) will degrade at least one QA metric relative to the full configuration, and the full configuration will beat the no-component baseline — i.e., each component earns its place and the whole exceeds the parts.

failure_condition: Fail (as a research program) if NO ablation degrades ANY metric beyond measurement noise — i.e., the full architecture is indistinguishable from the union of its ablations, meaning the components are decorative. Also fail if the full condition does not beat the baseline on at least one of accuracy/Brier/ECE (the architecture as a whole adds nothing).

limitations: Single ablations only; cannot detect redundancy or interaction effects (needs factorial design). The QA task is provider-knowledge-dominated, so effect sizes may be small and noisy at 5 trials. 'Beats the baseline' is a low bar since the baseline lacks memory entirely. This protocol is a component-necessity screen, not a sufficiency or synergy proof — and it says nothing about consciousness; it is an engineering evaluation of a cognitive architecture.
